_doc: (regex, tier, family). Tier drives the base score; family drives --family.
A tier-0 title is invisible, not merely ranked low: title_match()
returns the MAX tier among matching rules, so adding a rule here can
only ever raise a posting's tier, never lower it. That is what makes
this list safe to extend - and why every widening below records what
it cost, measured over a real 56,524-posting snapshot.
`note` is the justification, kept with the rule rather than in a
commit message. A rule whose reasoning has been lost is a rule
nobody can safely change.

note: Covers "dev ops" with a space and the whole devsecops family. Measured
on 205 distinct titles from a fortnight of real alert mail: 15
infra-shaped titles scored tier 0, and SIX were caught by widening this
one rule - "DevSecOps Engineer", "Senior DevSecOps Engineer", "Cloud
Security DevSecOps Engineer", "Azure DevSecOps Architect", "Dev Ops I"
and "Dev Ops II, Public Cloud". A tier-0 title never reaches scoring at
all, so these were invisible rather than ranked low.
`ops` keeps its word boundary so "operations" cannot match, and bare
"secops" is deliberately excluded - that is a SOC analyst title, and
analyst roles are out by request. Costs 21 extra postings across a
56,524-posting snapshot, nearly all of them genuine DevSecOps reqs.
Adjacency with at most one word between, which is what "Kubernetes
(K8S) / HPC Engineer" needs - four characters of punctuation and one
token sit between the platform and the role noun. Bounded deliberately:
the unbounded "kubernetes anywhere AND engineer anywhere" form admitted
19 postings, mostly "Senior Software Engineer - Python/Golang -
Kubernetes" coding roles, while this one admits exactly 1 extra posting
in 56,524 and still rescues the title it was written for.
"Platform Administration Lead", "Data Platform Operations Engineer".
The power-platform lookbehind is load-bearing: "Power BI & Power
Platform Administrator" is an M365 reporting role, and it arrived in the
same fortnight of mail as the titles above. Requiring the role noun
(operations ENGINEER, or administrator/administration) rather than a
bare "platform operations" is what keeps out "Sr Program Manager, GTM
Platform Operations" and the support-engineer variants - the loose form
admitted 32 postings of which 22 were program-manager or support roles.
"Manager, AMS/SAP Platform Administration and Support" still matches but
is harmless: level_of reads it as exec, which is -10.
A gap is allowed between "cloud" and "operations" because vendors put
their product name there: "VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Operations
Engineer". Admits 0 extra postings in the 56,524-posting snapshot, so
the widening is free - the title it rescues came through alert mail from
a board the radar does not poll.

rules.section: family: adjacent (infra work that hires from support)
family: vendor (only counts at a DevOps tool vendor)

note: `sales` was removed on 2026-10-29, after the only tracked row this entire
vendor family has ever produced turned out to be one nobody wanted: a
Fivetran "Sales Engineer, Enterprise". Measured against all 80 tracker rows,
every other vendor rule - support engineer, customer success, escalation,
implementation, onboarding, deployment, TAM, professional services,
developer advocate - has produced ZERO. Nine rules and 85 vendor names, and
the family's lifetime output was that one sales job.
The mechanism is worth keeping in mind for any future vendor rule. A vendor
title reaches the notify threshold on its title ALONE:
tier 3 x 3 = 9  +  vendor bonus 4  +  level mid 2  =  15
and 15 is exactly --notify-min-score. The Fivetran req's Terraform and
Kubernetes mentions took it from 15 to 23 - they made the alert loud, they
did not cause it. No technical evidence was ever required.
`solutions` and `field` are kept. Both are hands-on pre-sales engineering
rather than a quota-carrying track, both are the original intent of the
vendor path (support/solutions work at a DevOps tool vendor converting into
SRE), and both have produced zero rows so far - so keeping them costs
nothing measured and removing them would gain nothing measured either.
Revisit if either one ever produces a surprise of its own.

_doc: Subjects that are not this profession. The ONE thing in this file that
can LOWER a tier - everything else is additive, because title_match
returns the max tier among matching rules, so a new rule can only
promote a posting. That property is what makes the rules safe to
extend without re-testing, and the veto breaks it.
A group is {name, subject, rescue}: `subject` names what the job is
ABOUT, `rescue` is that subject's escape hatch. Each group carries its
OWN rescue, because a token that proves a water job is really IT does
not prove it of a finance job - 'it' and 'platform' rescue the first
and ruin the second. Order does not matter; the first group whose
subject matches and whose rescue does not wins, and the group name is
reported so a suppression is countable rather than silent.
Adding a group is the expensive kind of change. Measure it against the
real titles in `seen` and both nearmiss tables first, and record the
before/after in the group's note like the three below do.

groups.name: civil-infrastructure
note: The ONE thing in this file that can LOWER a tier. Everything else is
additive - title_match returns the max tier among matching rules, so a
new rule can only promote a posting. That property is what makes the
list safe to extend without re-testing, and this breaks it, so it is
deliberately one pattern with one escape hatch rather than a second
rule system.
Why it exists: on 2026-10-29 a 'Water/Wastewater Infrastructure
Specialist' at the Government of Alberta alerted at score 16. It is a
municipal civil-engineering job. The rule it satisfied is
'(cloud|infrastructure|infra) (engineer|...|specialist)' at tier 4, and
it is not wrong - 'infrastructure' is core DevOps vocabulary AND core
civil-engineering vocabulary. 12 from the tier, +2 mid, +2 for the word
'escalation' somewhere in the JD, and it cleared the notify threshold of
15 by one point.
`subject` names what the job is ABOUT - water, roads, HVAC, buildings -
not how it is done. `rescue` keeps anything carrying a real IT token, so
'Cloud Infrastructure Specialist' at the same employer still matches.
Measured before shipping, against 531 distinct real titles from `seen`
and both nearmiss tables, of which 395 are admitted by the gate today:
5 are vetoed and 0 relevant titles are lost. The five are the water
role, two 'Building Automation' roles at the University of Toronto (that
is HVAC controls), 'ELECTRICAL SYSTEMS ENGINEER' at the City of Toronto
and 'Satellite Electrical Systems Engineer' at Scalian.
`rescue` deliberately omits bare 'systems', 'technology' and 'network'.
An earlier draft included 'systems' and those four building/electrical
titles survived it - a facilities title uses that word exactly as often
as an IT one. It also omits 'infrastructure' itself, which would rescue
the posting that prompted all this.
Note the words NOT here: 'pipeline' (CI/CD), 'platform', 'automation'.
'pipeline' would veto every data and deployment pipeline title in the
search, which is the single most expensive mistake available in this
pattern.

groups.name: business-function
note: A business function, not an engineering discipline. On 2026-10-31 a
'Customer Success Platform Administrator' at Braze alerted at 17 and a
'Finance Systems Analyst - Integrations and Automation' at 1Password at
15. Same shape as the civil group: 'platform' and 'systems' belong to
two professions and the admitting rule only knows one. Note the
platform rule already carried a '(?<!power )' lookbehind, bolted on
when 'Power Platform Administrator' got through - a one-word lookbehind
cannot generalise, which is why this is a subject group instead.
`rescue` here is DELIBERATELY TIGHTER than the civil group's. It omits
'it', 'platform', 'software', 'database' and 'cyber', every one of
which appears in the titles this group exists to drop: the civil
rescue would have saved 'IT Operations Analyst' and 'Customer Success
Platform Administrator' outright. A rescue list is per-subject, not
global, and that is the reason the veto is a list of groups.
Measured against 544 distinct real titles (381 admitted): 10 vetoed,
0 relevant titles lost. A 'Salesforce DevOps Engineer' or an 'SAP
Basis Administrator, Azure' still matches - the rescue carries devops
and azure.
'clinical' and 'pharmaceutical' were in the first draft and were taken
out before shipping: they name an INDUSTRY, not a function, and a DevOps
job at a hospital is still a DevOps job. 'clinical' alone cost 'IT
Infrastructure Services 4 - Clinical Critical Messaging', a real
infrastructure role, and everything the pair caught legitimately was
already caught by support-analyst. Keep this list to what a team DOES.
Words here that catch nothing in today's 544 titles, kept as the obvious
next arrivals rather than because they were measured: customer
experience, crm, accounting, payroll, people operations, talent,
recruiting, marketing, sales, legal, workday.
`engineer` is in the rescue, and it is not slack. On 2026-10-31 the test
suite caught this group vetoing 'Customer Success Engineer' at a vendor -
a DELIBERATELY KEPT tier-4 title, the support path the whole vendor family
exists for and the one closest to Harman's six years of support work. The
group targets business-function ADMINISTRATION - analysts, administrators,
consultants - not engineering inside a business domain. Costs nothing
measured: all 10 titles this group drops are Analyst, Administrator or
Consultant roles, none of them an engineer.
groups.subject: \b(customer\s+success|customer\s+experience|crm|salesforce|finance|financial|accounting|payroll|procurement|billing|treasury|benefits|hr|human\s+resources|people\s+operations|talent|recruit\w*|marketing|sales|legal|supply\s+chain|workday|netsuite|sap)\b

groups.name: support-analyst
note: Analyst titles. Harman's standing instruction is 'I don't want IT
support or analys jobs in my tracker, please don't add those in the
rules' - but they were never coming in through one rule to remove.
Measured on 2026-10-31: 69 admitted analyst titles arrive through SIX
different rules, 49 of them through '(linux|unix|systems?)
(engineer|administrator|admin|analyst)' alone, the rest through the
cloud/infra, endpoint, it-operations, noc and reliability rules.
Tightening six admitting rules by hand is the version of this fix that
rots, so it is a subject group - which is also the only mechanism that
can express 'analyst' as a disqualifier independent of the rule that
admitted it.
Five had reached the tracker, all still `toapply`, none applied:
Fivetran 'IT Operations Analyst II' (24), Braze (17), Purolator 'IT
Operations & CMDB Analyst' (17), TD Bank 'IT Operations Analyst II'
(16), 1Password (15).
Scope was chosen explicitly, knowing the cost: four borderline titles
go with them - 'Sr. Analyst, Application Reliability Engineering',
'Sr IT Operations Analyst - Cisco UCS & VMware', 'Senior Endpoint
Security Operations Analyst' and 'Application & Infrastructure
Analyst'. The rescue therefore omits vmware, endpoint, reliability and
bare infrastructure ON PURPOSE. Widen it here, not in the subject, if
that judgement changes.
'analyst' is the whole subject because the word is the disqualifier.
A short pattern is not a truncated one: the loader proves each group
against canary titles rather than measuring its length.
groups.subject: \banalyst\b
